At the strategic level, a PLAN expansion into the ‘white-water’ of the icebound Arctic would seem to make sense for an outward-looking Chinese government seeking to develop Arctic resources and sea-lanes and project power beyond its near seas. Nuclear deterrence, sea-denial, commerce defence, and political leverage have all been held out by commentators as broad strategic objectives achievable with an Arctic submarine presence. What is missing from this discussion, however, is a more nuanced operational analysis of the real costs, benefits, technical challenges, and geophysical hazards inherent to sending submarines under the ice to threaten American and Western interests. As the US Navy learned during the Cold War, working and fighting in the Arctic is not a straightforward proposition

This article is not an attempt to divine Chinese intent for the Arctic, nor is it a study of China’s understanding and weighting of the region’s strategic importance. The broader political analysis has been done elsewhere and that debate continues.Footnote5 Rather, this piece addresses the under-examined operational challenges that would face China in the Arctic. How effective would Chinese submarines really be in the polar waters and what limitations of geography and hydrography might come into play? At the strategic level, we game out some of the more commonly discussed rationales for a Chinese polar presence,
examining in detail what PLAN boats might actually hope to accomplish in the North during both peace and wartime.
offer an assessment of the threat which Chinese submarines could realistically pose to the United States and Western interests from the Arctic.

This is not to assume that China’s future behaviour will fit neatly into our ‘logical’ weighting of costs and benefits. Beijing’s priorities, perceptions, and goals are often different than what Western observers assume. Short of action or clear policy direction from the Chinese government there will continue to be a fog of uncertainty over that country’s intentions. Despite this, the fact that the US Navy now officially anticipates ‘Chinese Navy deployments on, below, and above Arctic waters’, suggests that the time has come to consider not just whether China is seeking an Arctic naval presence but how it might proceed, against whom that presence may be directed, and – most importantly – how dangerous it would be.

Over the past decade China’s naval focus and capabilities have expanded dramatically, with the PLAN rapidly transformed from a coastal defence force into a powerful blue water fleet, even surpassing the US Navy in sheer number of combatants.Footnote6 Shipbuilding patterns over the past decade indicate China’s most pressing security interests remain centred on the waters within the first island chain, which runs from the edges of the South and East China Seas to Japan. However, it has grown its power projection capabilities and official policy is increasingly global in outlook. China’s 2015 naval strategy notably included ‘far seas protection’ as a new security consideration.Footnote7 That same year, the state’s National Security Law added the polar region as an area of strategic value to China for ‘peaceful exploration and use’ and ‘preserving the security of [the] nation’s activities.’Footnote8

China’s nuclear submarine fleet remains small but has been steadily modernising, which is most evident in the commissioning of its six Type 094/Jin-class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines (SSBNs), superseding the single ‘symbolic’ Xia-class that has been in the inventory since the 1980s.Footnote9 The Jin-class, based in Hainan Island at the northern edge of the South China Sea, provides China with the undersea leg of its nuclear deterrent triad, though their relative noisiness makes them much less secure for the second-strike role than the SSBNs of countries like Russia and the United States.Footnote10 The heart of the PLAN’s nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN) fleet are the six Type 093/Shang-class, which are separated into three variants: the first two baseline models followed by an unknown mix of the improved Type 093A and Type 093B.Footnote11 The Shangs superseded the five Type 091 Han-class SSNs built between 1970 and 1990, of which perhaps three remain in service.Footnote12 By US Office of Naval Intelligence estimates, the PLAN will operate seven SSNs by the end of 2020 – a fairly minor net growth from five in 2000 that stands in marked contrast to its net doubling of destroyers, frigates, and corvettes during the same period.Footnote13

There are, however, signs that the PLAN SSN fleet could double over the next decade.Footnote14 With the conclusion of Shang-class construction, observers are waiting on further revelations of the latest SSN, the Type 095. Although not much is confirmed so far, various Chinese sources have revealed disparate pieces of ‘new’ submarine technologies that Western observers suspect will be incorporated into the Type 095.Footnote15 These include a shaftless propeller, a single (rather than double) hull, and integrated electric propulsion.Footnote16 It has also been classified as a nuclear-powered guided missile submarine (SSGN) by the American intelligence community, denoting a boat with a significant cruise missile capability.Footnote17 If these missiles have a long-range land-attack capability akin to the American Tomahawks, it would suggest China is expanding its undersea missions to include power projection on a much wider geographic scale. It remains uncertain how many Type 095 or follow-on designs will be built, but if the surface fleet is any indication, a successful design could result in a long serial production run, resulting in a much greater proportion of the Chinese submarine fleet capable of covert global power projection. Regardless of the specific capabilities of the Type 095, satellite imagery has clearly shown a wholescale reconstruction and modernisation of China’s sole nuclear submarine construction yard in Bohai, indicating Chinese dedication to expanding the size and capability of its nuclear-powered submarine fleet.Footnote18 Although insufficient of itself, such a development in fleet numbers would be the first and most basic condition for an enduring Chinese underwater presence in the Arctic.

In 2018 it released a white paper describing itself as a ‘Near-Arctic State’, with a vested interest in northern resources, shipping, fisheries, and regional governance.Footnote19 Tens of billions of dollars have flowed from Chinese banks, state-owned enterprises, and the Silk Road fund into Arctic pipelines, offshore drilling, and liquid natural gas projects. The incentive is clear: shipping through an ice free (or ice-diminished) Arctic could save ships travelling between China and Europe 3,700 km (through the Northern Sea Route) or 3,800 km from China to the US Eastern Seaboard (through the Northwest Passage).Footnote20 While this scenario is years away, Chinese commentators have clearly recognised that accessing Arctic routes would not only save time and fuel but move shipping routes away from the sometimes dangerous waters off Africa and Malaysia and avoid the strategic chokepoint at the Strait of Malacca. The warming Arctic may also offer lucrative new fishing grounds as southern species migrate north with the warming waters. Chinese interest in these fisheries was clearly demonstrated by its participation in the 2018 Arctic Fisheries Agreement. As one of only three non-Arctic states to sign on to develop sustainable northern fisheries, Beijing has placed itself in a leadership role in that governance forum.

What is missing from China’s Arctic policy is a clear picture of what, if any, security interests the country has in the region. The National Security Law’s reference to the polar regions is ambiguous; meanwhile, the artfully crafted white paper mentions security concerns only in passing, and always in reference to China’s desire to cooperate with Arctic countries to manage issues such as ‘maritime accidents, environmental pollution, and maritime crimes’.Footnote21 Whether the Arctic falls under the category of ‘far seas protection’ laid out in the 2019 defence strategy remains unstated.Footnote22

Lacking a clear idea of official Chinese thinking on hard security in the Arctic region, commentators have tended to take the work of Chinese scholars and PLAN officers at face value. Noted China expert Ann-Marie Brady, for instance, has made a point of relying heavily on Chinese language materials, given Beijing’s lack of transparency in foreign language publications. In seeking to decipher China’s intent for the Arctic, it has also been common practice to draw comparisons with its predatory behaviour and disregard for international law in areas like the South China Sea, using this as a template for the country’s designs on the North. When presenting evidence to a Canadian Senate Committee in 2019, one of this paper’s authors was surprised to encounter a senator convinced that China’s militarisation of the South China Sea naturally translated to a desire to control, or even annex, Arctic land and maritime space.Footnote26

connection Secretary Pompeo made at the 2019 Arctic Council ministerial in Rovaniemi, where he decried China’s global malfeasance, highlighting its challenges to international law in the East and South China Seas. ‘China’s pattern of behaviour in the Indo-Pacific region and its disregard for international law’, Pompeo told his audience of Arctic dignitaries, ‘are cause for concern as its economic and scientific presence in the Arctic grows’.Footnote27 Specifically, the Secretary foresaw a Chinese submarine presence in the region – drawing that conclusion from ‘China’s pattern of aggressive behaviour elsewhere’.Footnote28 Rhetorically, he asked ‘do we want the Arctic Ocean to transform into a new South China Sea, fraught with militarisation and competing territorial claims?’Footnote29

What might that militarisation look like? Parallels with the South China Sea can only be taken so far. While China’s bellicosity and disregard for its neighbours’ sovereignty in that area might indicate an attitude that could apply further abroad, the actual building of islands or the attempt to physically control the surrounding waters would not work in the Arctic, where the continental shelf is owned and controlled by superpowers and their allies. Instead, most scholars see the kind of
Chinese military presence outlined by Chinese writers as being tied less to regional control and more to the defence of Chinese economic and global strategic interests.

For instance, if the Arctic seas evolve into busy shipping lanes and rich fishing grounds China may need a presence to defend its commercial interests, threaten those of its enemies, and guarantee its say in regional governance. Brady considers this a natural evolution for the PLAN as it follows Mahan’s recipe for rising powers.Footnote30 Indeed, China has rapidly transformed from a continental power to one with an economy oriented to the sea through an extensive trading network. This need to defend its growing Arctic shipping and economic interests is, therefore, a common rationale for any future submarine deployment.Footnote31
